questions.prompt: What actually triggers a main-sequence star to become a red giant?
options: It runs out of hydrogen in its core
It runs out of gravity
A passing star knocks it off balance
It gets too hot and boils off
questions.explanation: After billions of years the core's hydrogen is fused into helium. Without that fusion pushing outward, gravity wins in the core — and the envelope responds by swelling, while a shell just outside the core starts burning the remaining hydrogen.
questions.misconception: It feels like a star grows as it adds energy, but the giant's swell is the signature of the core running dry: the missing furnace is what lets the envelope balloon.

questions.prompt: In a red giant, where does hydrogen fusion continue to happen?
options: In the very center, where it always did
In a thin shell wrapped around the helium core
Across the whole swollen envelope
Nowhere — the giant has no fusion at all
questions.explanation: The inert core is too hot for hydrogen but not yet hot enough for helium, so burning continues in a thin shell just outside the core — like a coal ring smoldering around a cold center.
questions.misconception: It's natural to picture the star's fusion staying wherever it started, but the scene moves: the only hydrogen left burns in a thin rind outside the dead center.

questions.prompt: Why does the red giant's surface look red instead of yellow-white?
options: Because its gas is dirty from dust
Because the envelope expanded, spread, and therefore cooled to about 3,000 K
Because red stars radiate more light overall
Because the core leaks red dye into the envelope
questions.explanation: The same gas spread over a far larger surface means each patch is thinner and cooler. A surface around 3,000 K radiates mostly in the red — exactly what color is a thermometer predicts.
questions.misconception: Red 'hot like a fire' intuition returns here — but the giant is cooler than the star it used to be; the red tells you the surface is failing to keep the old temperature.

questions.prompt: What will happen to the Sun in roughly five billion years?
options: Nothing — it will shine exactly as today forever
It will shrink into a small cool ball
It will swell into a red giant big enough to swallow Mercury and Venus
It will wander away from the solar system
questions.explanation: When its core hydrogen gives out, the Sun swells into a red giant whose surface reaches roughly the orbit of Earth — Mercury and Venus are engulfed; Earth's oceans boil even if it is not swallowed.
questions.misconception: The Sun feels permanent, but 'permanent' only lasts the main-sequence lifetime of ten billion years; the red giant stage arrives as surely as an alarm clock.

questions.prompt: Compared with its main-sequence size, a red giant is about how much larger?
options: A little bit larger — about 1.5 times
Hundreds of thousands of times larger
Dozens of times larger in diameter
About the same size but redder
questions.explanation: A Sun-like star swells to roughly 30 to 100 times its main-sequence radius — a volume many thousands of times larger, with the envelope correspondingly thin.
questions.misconception: The name 'giant' suggests maybe twice, but the slider in the model makes the real leap unforgettable: the old star would fit inside the red one dozens of times over.
